title: Montrose County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: In Montrose County, median well depth is 70 ft with typical yields around 10 gpm. Learn what that means for drilling cost and water reliability.
h1: Water wells in Montrose County, Colorado
intro_html:
Montrose County has a wide spread of well conditions, from shallow alluvial wells near the valley floors to deeper fractured-bedrock wells in the outlying country. County-wide records give you a good sense of how deep you may need to drill, what kind of yield to expect, and what a realistic budget looks like before you buy or build.

The numbers here are from Colorado Division of Water Resources permits for the whole county, including rural areas around Montrose, Olathe, Naturita, Nucla, Redvale and Colona.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Montrose County
sections.html:
Across Montrose County, the median well depth is only about 70 feet, but the middle half of wells ranges from 33 to 224 feet. That tells you the easy, shallow holes are mixed in with some substantially deeper ones. The 90th percentile sits at 358 feet, and the deepest recorded well goes down to 1,248 feet, so it is possible to chase water a long way in the wrong spot.

Most wells are relatively shallow: 56% are under 100 feet and another 28% fall between 100 and 300 feet. About 13% end up in the 300–600 foot range and 3% go beyond 600 feet. Expect valley locations to run on the shallower side, and higher, rockier ground to be more variable, especially in fractured-bedrock.

sections.heading: What well yields look like here
sections.html:
Yields in Montrose County are generally solid for domestic use. The median reported yield is 10 gpm, with the middle half of wells between 5 and 15 gpm. For a normal household, anything above 2–3 gpm is workable if the well is managed properly, so most wells here exceed that comfortably.

Still, there is a spread. About 3% of wells report under 1 gpm, which is a red flag for buyers, and 17% fall between 1 and 5 gpm. The bulk of wells, 52%, come in between 5 and 15 gpm, and 28% are 15 gpm or more. If you are evaluating a specific parcel, look closely at nearby well permits to see if your immediate area is in that stronger-yield group.

sections.heading: Water table depth and recent trends
sections.html:
Static water level, which is the depth from ground surface to the water in the well, has a median of 32 feet in Montrose County. The middle half of measurements runs from 17 down to 106 feet. That means some owners hit water practically near the surface, while others have to set pumps well over 100 feet down.

Looking by decade, the median depth to water was 22 feet in the 2000s, dropped deeper to 45 feet in the 2010s, then came back to 30 feet in the 2020s. With only 159 wells reporting static levels, that trend line should be taken cautiously, but it does suggest some fluctuation rather than a steady long-term drop. For a specific property, ask for recent measurements from the existing well, not just the original drilling log.

sections.heading: Who has been drilling in Montrose County
sections.html:
Montrose County has a long history of well development, with 3,926 permits on record and 2,130 listed as constructed. Drilling activity picked up sharply starting in the 1970s. There were 84 permits in the 1950s, 37 in the 1960s, then a jump to 273 in the 1970s and 274 in the 1980s.

Growth really showed in the 1990s and 2000s, with 693 and 820 permits respectively, followed by 495 in the 2010s and already 361 in the 2020s, with the newest permit issued in 2025. Most wells are in unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers, with smaller numbers in the Dakota and Dakota Sandstone formations. The busier drillers on record include Authorized (Pe, Pg), Valley Drilling Co. (Stoy, Kenneth), and Mccracken Well Drilling Inc (Mccracken, Alan E.).

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost here
sections.html:
In Montrose County’s mix of sedimentary and alluvial ground, typical drilling runs about $50–$75 per foot. At the county-wide median depth of 70 feet, that puts the drilled hole itself around $3,500–$5,200. That is just the borehole, not the full system.

By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a complete well system at that median depth usually lands in the $9,500–$17,200 range. If your area tends to run closer to the 224-foot upper end of the middle range, scale that budget up accordingly. Ask drillers bidding your job to show how their price changes if they have to go 100–200 feet deeper than planned.

sections.heading: Risks: low yield, contamination and site layout
sections.html:
Most wells are permitted for domestic or household use (49%), with a fair number for stock (13%) and irrigation (3%), plus a substantial monitoring-well presence (30%). A small share of domestic wells land under 1 gpm, so low-yield or marginal wells are a real, if not common, risk. In fractured-bedrock areas, yields can change sharply over short distances, so a neighbor’s good well is encouraging but not a guarantee.

There are also mapped environmental concerns: 28 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 7 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site within about 10 miles in the county. Before closing on land, match your location against these, plan proper well setback from septic, and make sure you have room for a conforming leach field along with access for a drilling rig.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a well in Montrose County
sections.html:
If you are buying an existing home on a well, pull the DWR permit, look at the total depth, reported yield, and any static water level readings. A 5–15 gpm well at typical Montrose County depths is usually adequate for a household, but you still want a current flow test and water-quality lab work, especially near mapped PFAS or historic mining areas.

For vacant land, study nearby wells around Montrose, Olathe, Nucla, Naturita, Redvale and Colona to see how deep they went and what they produce. Budget based on the deeper end of local depths, not the shallowest neighbor. In over-appropriated basins, expect to deal with augmentation plans if you need more than a standard exempt household well. Plan your driveway, building site, septic and well locations together so you do not box yourself into a bad drilling spot.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Montrose County, Colorado?
faq.a: County records show a median well depth of about 70 feet, with the middle half of wells between 33 and 224 feet deep. Most wells are relatively shallow: 56% are under 100 feet and another 28% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Around 13% extend to 300–600 feet, and a small minority, about 3%, go deeper than 600 feet, sometimes much deeper in tougher areas.

faq.q: What is a good well yield in Montrose County?
faq.a: In Montrose County the median reported yield is 10 gpm, and the middle half of wells fall between 5 and 15 gpm. For a typical household, anything above about 2–3 gpm can work with proper storage and management, so most wells here are comfortably above that. Still, around 3% of wells report under 1 gpm and 17% are in the 1–5 gpm range, so it is important to test a specific well.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Montrose County?
faq.a: With mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, typical drilling rates are about $50–$75 per foot. At the county’s 70-foot median depth, the borehole alone runs roughly $3,500–$5,200. A complete working well, including casing, pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical, often totals about $9,500–$17,200 at that depth. Deeper wells will scale up from there, so budget with a safety margin.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Montrose County?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. The county has 28 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 7 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site within about 10 miles, so some locations deserve extra scrutiny. Always test for bacteria, basic chemistry, and any contaminants of concern in your area before relying on a well for drinking water, and repeat tests periodically over time.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping in Montrose County wells?
faq.a: Reported static water levels show some ups and downs, not a clear steady decline. Median depth to water was about 22 feet in the 2000s, 45 feet in the 2010s, and 30 feet so far in the 2020s. Only 159 wells have static-level data, so that trend is somewhat limited, but it suggests fluctuations. For a property decision, ask for recent measurements and not just the original drilling records.
